lesson.text: Quick memory: why is the first search result not always the best? (Results are ranked by guesses, and some are adverts.) Today: checking what you find.
Anyone can put things online. Some of it is true, some is a mistake, some is made up, and some is trying to sell you something. Good readers check.
Ask three questions. Who wrote it: an expert, a museum, or someone you can't find out about? When: is it new, or old and out of date? Why: to inform, to sell, to persuade or to trick?
Check with other good sources. If two or three trusted sites say the same, it is more likely to be true. If only one strange site says it, be careful.
Facts can be checked; opinions can't (grade 3 English). Sharks have lived on Earth for over 400 million years is a fact you can check. Sharks are the best animals is an opinion.
Watch out for tricks: headlines that shout You won't believe this! Offers that are too good to be true, like a free tablet for everyone. And photos that have been changed.
Worked example: a page says octopuses have three hearts. Who wrote it? Scientists at an aquarium. Do other good sites agree? Yes: a museum's page says so too. So it is very likely true.
Try it in the world: find one surprising fact about our world, like how deep the sea is, and check it on two good sites. Did they agree? Next: data in tables.

exercises.prompt: Everything on the internet is true.
exercises.explain: False: anyone can, so some things are mistakes, made up or adverts. Check.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a fact, or an opinion?
items: The Moon goes round the Earth.
exercises.hint: Could you check it, or is it what someone thinks?
exercises.explain: Facts can be checked: three hearts, 0 °C, the Moon. Cutest, best and nicest are opinions.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best place to check a fact about sharks?
exercises.hint: Who knows most about sharks, and wants to tell the truth?
choices: a museum's or an aquarium's website
exercises.explain: Museums and aquariums have experts, and they want to inform, not sell or joke.

exercises.prompt: Why was this written? Buy Speedy Stripe shoes: they make you run twice as fast!
exercises.hint: What does it want you to do?
exercises.explain: It wants you to buy shoes: it was written to sell.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of checking a page in order.
exercises.hint: Read first; check with another site last.
items: Check it on another good site
exercises.explain: Read it, ask who, when and why, then check another good site.

exercises.prompt: A pop-up says you have won a free tablet and asks where you live. What is it?
exercises.hint: Is it too good to be true? Does it ask for personal information?
choices: a trick: close it and tell a grown-up
exercises.explain: It is too good to be true and it asks where you live: a trick. Close it and tell a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: An old page can be out of date, even if it was true when it was written.
exercises.explain: True: new discoveries change what we know, so check when a page was written.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to what it checks.
exercises.hint: Each question checks one thing about the page.
exercises.explain: Who: an expert? When: out of date? Why: inform, sell or trick? Others: do good sites agree?

exercises.prompt: A headline shouts: Scientists find a cat that can fly to the Moon! What should you think?
exercises.hint: Is it too amazing? Do trusted sites say it?
choices: it is almost certainly made up
it must be true: it's on a website
exercises.explain: It is too amazing to be true, and no trusted site would say it: almost certainly made up.

exercises.prompt: Two museums say an ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain. A stranger's comment says it isn't. Which do you trust more?
exercises.hint: Who are the experts? How many good sources agree?
exercises.explain: Two museums agree, and they have experts: trust them more. (It's true: an ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.)

exercises.prompt: Why might someone put a made-up story online?
choices: to get clicks, sell things or trick people
exercises.explain: Made-up stories get clicks, sell things or trick people.

exercises.prompt: A photo online can be changed to show something that never happened.
exercises.hint: Can pictures be edited on a computer?
exercises.explain: True: photos can be edited, so a photo alone doesn't prove something.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: more trustworthy, or be careful?
items: a page with no author and no date
exercises.explain: Museums, science magazines and expert encyclopedias are more trustworthy. Pages with no author, shouting headlines and prize pop-ups need care.

exercises.prompt: A page from 1998 says there are 9 planets. In 2006, scientists decided that Pluto is a dwarf planet. How many planets are there now?
exercises.hint: Which planet was taken off the list?
exercises.explain: Pluto became a dwarf planet in 2006: 9 − 1 = 8 planets. The 1998 page is out of date.
